extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety professionals, and stakeholders (notice-and-comment participants) affected by OSHA's proposed occupational heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the proposed regulatory criteria, scope, exemptions, triggers, definitions, and required controls in OSHA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking for prevention of heat-related injuries and illnesses. Useful for preparing comments, compliance planning, or analysis of the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold finding for promulgation
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must make a threshold finding that a significant risk of material harm exists, and that issuance of the new standard will substantially reduce that risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's preamble documents health effects, risk assessment, and evidence of risk reduction to support this finding (see Sections IV and V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material harm (heat-related injuries and illnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat-related injuries and illnesses (HRIs) often result in material harm because they can be disabling, cause lost work time, require medical treatment or restricted work, and in some cases cause death; they can reduce functional capacity and lead to traumatic injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA treats HRIs that result in lost work time and/or the need for medical care beyond first aid as clearly constituting material harm, but also recognizes that some HRIs that do not meet those thresholds can still be material in severe cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence categories indicating material impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveillance datasets that capture cases involving days away from work (BLS SOII), hospital discharge datasets (emergency/inpatient), and workers' compensation claims indicate HRIs that represent material impairment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inclusion criteria are used in OSHA's risk assessment to identify materially impairing HRIs; note that these datasets undercount some HRIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that reversible HRIs can be material
rubrics_metrics.description: Even HRIs that are reversible (with early intervention) can be debilitating and therefore constitute material harm, and may progress to permanent damage if not treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA relies on clinical progression (e.g., heat exhaustion progressing to heat stroke) and functional-capacity impacts to justify materiality beyond strict reporting thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant risk determination
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA preliminarily determines there exists a significant risk of material harm to workers from occupational exposure to heat, based on peer-reviewed studies, state/national statistics, and analysis of BLS and workers' compensation data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA compares observed incidence (e.g., average 40 heat-related deaths annually and 3,389 HRIs involving days away from work annually) and sector-specific working-lifetime incidence estimates to its historical standards for significant risk (including the 1/1000 threshold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of incidence rates and sector-specific working-lifetime estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA relies on a range of HRI incidence rates (working lifetime = 45 years) across sectors and industries to assess risk (e.g., agriculture: 234–1,737/100,000; construction: 63–545/100,000; utilities: 513/100,000; some industries much higher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA treats these as the best available evidence to support a finding of significant risk even where precise exposure-only estimates are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for underreporting and denominator bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Available datasets underestimate true risk because inclusion criteria exclude many HRIs and because population denominators often include unexposed workers (e.g., climate-controlled office workers), lowering apparent incidence among exposed workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA adjusts interpretation of BLS and other statistics recognizing underreporting and dilution by unexposed workers; see Section V.A. for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of risk reduction from workplace interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-reviewed studies and authoritative bodies indicate interventions (rest breaks, cool drinking water, acclimatization, shade, fans, etc.) substantially reduce heat strain and HRI risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily estimates implementation of the proposed standard would reduce HRIs by roughly 37–96% and heat-related fatalities by ~99.8–100% among covered employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope — who must comply (paragraph (a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All employers subject to OSHA jurisdiction—including general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture—must comply with the proposed requirements, subject to enumerated exemptions in paragraphs (a)(2) and (a)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed standard applies across indoor and outdoor work areas and various sectors; employers are responsible for determining which of their work activities are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer responsibility for activity-level coverage determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must determine which specific work activities are covered by the standard; some employers may have both exempt and covered activities and must apply the standard accordingly to covered activities/ employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an employer's employees exclusively perform exempt activities listed in (a)(2)(i)-(vi), the entire employer may be exempt under (a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — no reasonable expectation of exposure at or above the initial heat trigger (a)(2)(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work activities for which there is no reasonable expectation of exposure at or above the initial heat trigger are excluded from the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to operations inherently unlikely to reach the initial trigger (e.g., seasonal outdoor holiday market in winter where daily highs are always below the initial trigger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — short duration exposures (a)(2)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short duration employee exposures at or above the initial heat trigger of 15 minutes or less in any 60-minute period are excluded from the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily concluded exposures ≤15 minutes typically do not raise core body temperature by ≥1°C; cumulative exposures count (e.g., exiting an air‑conditioned vehicle repeatedly only exempt if cumulative exposure ≤15 minutes per 60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — organizations whose primary function is firefighting and certain emergency response activities (a)(2)(iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations whose primary function is firefighting are excluded; emergency response activities of workplace emergency response teams, EMS, and technical search and rescue, and activities already covered under cited standards, are excluded when performing emergency response activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's separate Emergency Response rulemaking is intended to cover heat hazards for responders; the exemption applies when employees are performing emergency response duties but not during their ordinary non-emergency duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — indoor work areas/vehicles with consistent AC below 80°F (a)(2)(iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work activities performed in indoor work areas or vehicles where air-conditioning consistently keeps the ambient temperature below 80°F are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer must ensure AC consistently maintains ambient <80°F; OSHA expects expeditious repairs if AC malfunctions; commenters asked whether the standard should specify how long AC can be out before exemption ceases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — telework (a)(2)(v)
rubrics_metrics.description: Telework (work done from home or another remote location of the employee's choosing) is excluded from this standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only activities conducted while teleworking are exempt; employer must comply with the standard when employee is on-site at employer facilities unless another exemption applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — sedentary indoor work activities (a)(2)(vi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedentary indoor work activities that only involve some combination of sitting, occasional standing and walking for brief periods, and occasional lifting of objects weighing less than 10 pounds are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Occasional’ means up to one-third of the workday (BLS, 2021); activities must be brief; exemption applies regardless of indoor temperature (OSHA seeks comment on whether to limit by an upper temperature threshold such as the high heat trigger). Examples include desk work and seated indoor vehicle operation (e.g., forklift) if duties do not include heavier lifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer-wide exemption when all employees exclusively perform exempt activities (a)(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employer's employees exclusively perform the activities listed in paragraphs (a)(2)(i)–(vi), the employer is exempt from the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an employer whose entire workforce either teleworks or always works inside with AC consistently below 80°F would be exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA's requests for public comment on scope/exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA solicits comments and evidence on whether certain emergency response activities should be covered, how to handle AC system malfunctions and duration before exemption ends, whether sedentary work definition is appropriate and whether to limit it by an upper temperature threshold, and whether sedentary exemption should extend to outdoor work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are specific points commenters should address with evidence; they indicate areas where OSHA may revise exemption language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Acclimatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Acclimatization means the body's adaptation to work in the heat as a person is exposed to heat gradually over time, which reduces strain and enables safer work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included because proposed paragraph (e)(7) requires employers to implement one of two acclimatization protocols for new and returning employees when the initial heat trigger is met; employers must implement protocols at no cost to employees and train that lack of acclimatization is a risk factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Ambient temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambient temperature means the temperature of the air surrounding a body (air temperature or dry bulb temperature), measured by a standard thermometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined because it is used in heat index and WBGT definitions and in multiple proposed paragraphs (scope, identifying hazards, requirements at triggers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Cooling personal protective equipment (PPE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooling PPE means equipment worn to protect the user against heat-related injury or illness (e.g., bandanas, neck wraps, clothing with phase change materials or water-absorbent crystals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition clarifies requirement in proposed paragraph (e)(1) that if employer provides cooling PPE, the cooling properties must be maintained during use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Heat index
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat index means the National Weather Service heat index, combining ambient temperature and humidity to indicate how hot it feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools for measurement include OSHA‑NIOSH Heat Safety Tool app, phone weather apps, NOAA Heat Index Calculator for indoors, and monitoring devices; heat index is used to define initial and high heat triggers and other provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Initial heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial heat trigger means a heat index of 80°F or a WBGT equal to the NIOSH Recommended Alert Limit (RAL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposures at or above the initial heat trigger require implementation of controls under proposed paragraph (e) including drinking water, break areas, indoor work area controls, acclimatization of new/returning employees, rest breaks if needed, effective communication, and maintenance of cooling PPE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — High heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: High heat trigger means a heat index of 90°F or a WBGT equal to the NIOSH Recommended Exposure Limit (REL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposures at or above the high heat trigger require additional controls beyond the initial trigger, including required rest breaks, observation for signs and symptoms, hazard alerts, and warning signs for excessively high heat areas; scientific basis explained in Section V.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Indoor/indoors
rubrics_metrics.description: Indoors means an area under a ceiling or overhead covering that restricts airflow and has along its entire perimeter walls, doors, windows, dividers, or other barriers that restrict airflow (whether open or closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: garage even if door open, warehouse interior even if loading dock doors open, sheds with four walls and a ceiling; construction inside a structure after walls and roof are erected counts as indoors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Outdoor/outdoors
rubrics_metrics.description: Outdoors means an area that is not indoors as defined above; vehicles operated outdoors are considered outdoor work areas unless exempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include agricultural fields and canopies; used in identifying hazards and training provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Radiant heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Radiant heat means heat transferred by electromagnetic waves between surfaces (sources include sun, hot objects, liquids, surfaces, fire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included because radiant heat contributes to WBGT and is relevant to identifying heat hazards, e.g., furnaces, ovens, and combustion sources in foundries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Recommended Alert Limit (RAL)
rubrics_metrics.description: RAL means the NIOSH-recommended heat stress alert limits for unacclimatized workers (incorporates environmental WBGT and metabolic workload; assumes conventional one-layer clothing unless adjusted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA proposes to incorporate NIOSH Publication No. 2016-106 by reference; formula: RAL [°C–WBGT] = 59.9 - 14.1 log10 M[W], where M is metabolic rate in watts; used to set the initial heat trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Recommended Exposure Limit (REL)
rubrics_metrics.description: REL means the NIOSH-recommended heat stress exposure limits for acclimatized workers (used to set the high heat trigger when WBGT equals the NIOSH REL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA proposes to incorporate NIOSH guidance by reference; REL accounts for environmental factors and workload for acclimatized employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the initial heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: When the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded, employers must implement controls including drinking water, break area(s) for indoor and outdoor sites, indoor work area controls, acclimatization of new/returning employees, rest breaks if needed to prevent overheating, effective communication, and maintenance of cooling PPE properties if PPE is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are baseline protections that must be in place once the initial trigger is reached; specific provisions and implementation details appear in proposed paragraph (e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the high heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: When the high heat trigger is met or exceeded, additional controls are required such as mandated rest breaks, observation for signs and symptoms of HRI, hazard alerts, and warning signs for excessively high heat areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High heat trigger invokes more protective measures than initial trigger; see proposed paragraph (f) and Section VII.F. for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization protocol requirement for new and returning employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must implement one of two acclimatization protocols for new and returning employees when the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded; protocols must be implemented at no cost to the employee and training must cover that lack of acclimatization is a risk factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed paragraph (e)(7) specifies this requirement and paragraph (j) addresses employer cost; training obligation is in proposed paragraph (h)(1)(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and tools for heat index and WBGT
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA recognizes use of the National Weather Service heat index and tools such as the OSHA‑NIOSH Heat Safety Tool app, phone-based weather apps for outdoor areas, the NOAA Heat Index Calculator for indoor work areas, and monitoring devices that report heat index and/or WBGT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools are mentioned as practical methods for employers to measure triggers (initial/high) and implement the standard's requirements.
